pages.task: A flywheel of 2 kg m² feels 50 N m of net torque. How fast does its speed rise?
pages.why: Angular acceleration = net torque ÷ inertia = 50 ÷ 2 = 25 rad/s². It keeps rising at that rate for as long as the torques stay unbalanced.

pages.name: Two torques
pages.text: A set on its own makes whatever power its load draws. The alternator pulls back on the shaft with a torque equal to power ÷ speed. The engine drives it forward. While the two torques match, the speed holds. Any gap goes into or out of the spinning mass. The governor compares the speed with its set point and moves the fuel. It is the AVR's loop again, with fuel in place of field. Here the set point steps 1 Hz up and back. The fuel moves first, then the speed.

pages.task: The set runs alone at 60 Hz with no load. A load of 25% lands all at once. The governor is working. What does the frequency do?
pages.why: The load's torque arrives at once. The fuel takes time to follow. Until it does, the gap slows the spinning mass. So the frequency dips. Then the fuel catches up and the speed climbs back.

pages.task: The load's torque has jumped by 668 N m. The fuel has not moved yet. The shaft carries 20 kg m². How fast does the set slow?
pages.why: 668 ÷ 20 = 33.4 rad/s². In the 0.1 s before the fuel moves, the set loses 33.4 × 0.1 = 3.34 rad/s. That is 1.8% of 188.5 rad/s. The frequency follows the speed. So by 0.1 s it has fallen 1.8% too, from 60 to 58.9 Hz. It goes on falling until the engine's torque matches the load's again.

pages.task: An isochronous set runs at 60 Hz with 50% load. The load steps up to 75%. Once it settles, what has changed?
pages.why: Holding the speed needs the engine's torque to match the load's. A bigger load needs more torque, so more fuel. The governor brings the frequency back to 60 Hz. The fuel settles at 75%.

pages.text: The set point now sits at 62.4 Hz, chosen to give 60 Hz on full load. With 4% droop the line tilts down from 62.4 Hz at no load to 60 Hz at full load. pages.task: With 4% droop, this set runs at 62.4 Hz with no load and 60 Hz at full load, 504 kW. What frequency does it settle at with 252 kW?
pages.why: 252 ÷ 504 = 0.5. The line falls 2.4 Hz from no load to full load. So by half load it has fallen 1.2 Hz. 62.4 − 1.2 = 61.2 Hz.

pages.name: The set point
pages.text: The set point lifts the whole line without tilting it. So it picks the load at which the set runs at 60 Hz. Droop has a cost on a set alone. Its frequency moves with its load. Its use shows when two sets share one load. When all the load trips, the trace overshoots. Then the dot settles at the top of its line, its set point, here 62.4 Hz. That is above 60 Hz.

pages.task: A set on 4% droop runs at 60.0 Hz with no load. On full load it settles at 57.6 Hz. Fault or design?
pages.why: 4% of 60 Hz is 2.4 Hz. 60.0 − 2.4 = 57.6 Hz. That is exactly on its line. The governor is doing what it was set to do. Raise the set point to 62.4 Hz and full load lands on 60 Hz.

pages.name: A 50 Hz set
pages.task: Another set makes 50 Hz. It has 5% droop and runs at 50 Hz on full load. All its load trips. What frequency does it settle at?
pages.why: 5% of 50 Hz is 2.5 Hz. Full load sits at 50 Hz. So no load sits at 50 + 2.5 = 52.5 Hz. The frequency overshoots first, then settles there.
